title: Amazon RDS Overview
description: Understand RDS instance classes, storage options, and how they fit ASP.NET Core apps.

data.text: Amazon RDS is a managed relational database service. It supports SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, and Amazon Aurora, handling provisioning, patching, backups, and failover.

items: **DB instance** — a running database with specified CPU, memory, and storage
**DB instance class** — the compute and memory capacity (e.g., db.t3.micro)
**Storage** — gp2, gp3, or io1/io2 for high-performance workloads
**Multi-AZ** — synchronous standby replica in another Availability Zone

rows: Existing .NET apps familiar with SQL Server
Modern .NET apps with EF Core or Dapper

data.title: Create an RDS SQL Server instance
data.content:
Use the AWS CLI to create the infrastructure.
# Expected output: DB instance is created and becomes available within minutes.
data.code: aws rds create-db-instance --db-instance-identifier aspnet-db --db-instance-class db.t3.micro --engine sqlserver-express --allocated-storage 20 --master-username admin --master-user-password 'YourSecurePassword123!' --region us-east-1

data.title: Free tier
data.text: The AWS Free Tier includes 750 hours per month of db.t3.micro or db.t2.micro usage for SQL Server Express, PostgreSQL, or MySQL for 12 months.

items.question: Should I use SQL Server or PostgreSQL on RDS?
items.answer: Use SQL Server if you have existing SQL Server skills or need Windows authentication. PostgreSQL is open source and works well with EF Core and Dapper.

items.question: How do I back up RDS?
items.answer: RDS automatically creates daily snapshots and supports point-in-time recovery. You can also export snapshots to S3.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: RDS is a managed relational database service
Choose the engine based on your app's data needs
Enable Multi-AZ for production high availability
data.takeaway: RDS removes database administration overhead while keeping the familiar SQL programming model for C# developers.
